= 2x+1$ over the interval $[1,3].$ What is the height of the rectangle defined over the same interval that has the same area as $\textrm{R}?$ 

![](images/01/01597200b1f0e147fa8c53b6301d0c8e37208b5a6cce64cf0d9859d1220d8385.png)

Using the formula for the area of a trapezoid, we have that

$$
\eqalign{
\textrm{Area}\,(\textrm{R}) = \dfrac{1}{2}(3+7)(3-1)= 10.}
$$

For the rectangle to have the same area, we must have 

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =f(c)(3-1) \\ f(c) & =5 \\ 2c+1 & =5 \\ c & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can summarize what we've just done by saying that

$$
\int_1^3 (2x +1)\, \textrm d x= f(2) \cdot (3-1).
$$

This is an example of the **mean value theorem for integrals**, which states:

> *If $f(x)$ is a continuous function on the closed interval $[a, b]$, then there exists a number $c$ in that interval such that*
> 
> 
> $$
> \int_a^b f(x)\, \textrm d x = f(c) \cdot (b-a).
> $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c1b3241c-c8fd-514f-aa8c-a000710896d4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 986 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d75b1c61-1292-5625-8252-d8c10bae2e1b" :step/math-academy-id 618889 :step/next {:db/id 17592186101909}} {:db/id 17592186101909 :step/content {:db/id 17592186101021 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186100733 :question/id #uuid "a0f21b4c-0f5c-5567-aaec-9da481d2e7ac" :question/math-academy-id "e-547"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "86221215-32a6-5c5a-bcd7-220e166bcee8" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048187} {:db/id 17592186050819}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186101335} {:db/id 17592186101336} {:db/id 17592186101382} {:db/id 17592186256385} {:db/id 17592186256391} {:db/id 17592186290568} {:db/id 17592186290569} {:db/id 17592186290572} {:db/id 17592186290575} {:db/id 17592186290580} {:db/id 17592186317508}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Points That Satisfy the Mean Value Theorem for Integrals"} :step/id #uuid "3e6aeea7-0134-5101-a19a-c37ab846bb82" :step/math-academy-id 618890 :step/next {:db/id 17592186101910}} {:db/id 17592186101910 :step/content {:db/id 17592186102035 :tutorial/content "The **average value** of a continuous function on a closed interval $[a,b]$ is given by

= 2x+1$ over the interval $[1,3].$ What is the height of the rectangle defined over the same interval that has the same area as $\textrm{R}?$ 

![](images/01/01597200b1f0e147fa8c53b6301d0c8e37208b5a6cce64cf0d9859d1220d8385.png)

Using the formula for the area of a trapezoid, we have that

$$
\eqalign{
\textrm{Area}\,(\textrm{R}) = \dfrac{1}{2}(3+7)(3-1)= 10.}
$$

For the rectangle to have the same area, we must have 

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =f(c)(3-1) \\ f(c) & =5 \\ 2c+1 & =5 \\ c & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

We can summarize what we've just done by saying that

$$
\int_1^3 (2x +1)\, \textrm d x= f(2) \cdot (3-1).
$$

This is an example of the **mean value theorem for integrals**, which states:

> *If $f(x)$ is a continuous function on the closed interval $[a, b]$, then there exists a number $c$ in that interval such that*
> 
> 
> $$
> \int_a^b f(x)\, \textrm d x = f(c) \cdot (b-a).
> $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c1b3241c-c8fd-514f-aa8c-a000710896d4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 986 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d75b1c61-1292-5625-8252-d8c10bae2e1b" :step/math-academy-id 618889 :step/next {:db/id 17592186101909}} {:db/id 17592186102034 :tutorial/content "The region $\textrm{R},$ shown below, is the area under the graph of $f(x) = 2x+1$ over the interval $[1,3].$ What is the height of the rectangle defined over the same interval that has the same area as $\textrm{R}?$

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =|\begin{aligned}k & 2 & 1 \\ -2 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =k\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}|-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}|+1\cdot |\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =k(-1\cdot 2-1\cdot 1)-2(-2\cdot 2-(-1)\cdot 1)+(-2\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot (-1)) \\  & =-3k+6-3 \\  & =-3k+3.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =0 \\ -3k+3 & =0 \\ k & =1\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =(2i+j+k)-(3i-j+2k) \\  & =-i+2j-k \\  & =⟨-1,2,-1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =(-i+2j+k)-(3i-j+2k) \\  & =-4i+3j-k \\  & =⟨-4,3,-1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AD} & =d-a \\  & =(4i+4j+2k)-(3i-j+2k) \\  & =i+5j \\  & =⟨1,5,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the volume of the parallelepiped, we need to take the absolute value of the triple product of the above vectors.

Computing the triple product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot (\overset{\to }{AC}\times \overset{\to }{AD}) & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & -1 \\ -4 & 3 & -1 \\ 1 & 5 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}|-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}-4 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}|+(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}| \\  & =-(3\cdot 0-5\cdot (-1))-2((-4)\cdot 0-1\cdot (-1))-((-4)\cdot 5-1\cdot 3) \\  & =-5-2+23 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the corresponding parallelepiped spanned by $\overrightarrow{AB},$ $\overrightarrow{AC},$ and $\overrightarrow{AD}$ is

$$
V=|16|=16.

To illustrate, consider the parallelepiped shown below. The sides of this parallelepiped are formed by the vectors $\mathbf{a},$ $\mathbf{b},$ and $\mathbf{c}.$

![](images/25/2597b48a010607fca71c551dbce8e9e2bbeda47d0892a582347ae1cdf19f1bf6.png)

The volume of this parallelepiped is given by the absolute value of the triple product:

$$

$$

When we have three coplanar vectors, the parallelepiped they span is *flat* on the plane, and therefore its volume is zero. Consequently, the triple product of the vectors is zero as well.

So, if three vectors are coplanar, then their triple product is zero. The converse is also true: if the triple product of three nonzero vectors is zero, then the vectors are coplanar.

Therefore, we have the following statement:

> $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b},$ and $\mathbf{c}$ are coplanar $\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad$ $\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c}) = 0$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e3012c88-77aa-5271-ad5f-b2176f99ba15" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2957 :tutorial/title "The Volume Spanned by Coplanar Vectors"} :step/id #uuid "04e9769b-9cba-55d2-a3b5-ab09464bb0b3" :step/math-academy-id 464358 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106928}} {:db/id 17592186106928 :step/content {:db/id 17592186105908 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186105597 :question/id #uuid "c6f2dacc-11b0-5689-97d9-e1869c64aae1" :question/math-academy-id "e-4351"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "26c84e5b-97a7-5116-a90c-e4f011e87cf0" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048673}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186106094} {:db/id 17592186106095} {:db/id 17592186262894} {:db/id 17592186262898} {:db/id 17592186262899} {:db/id 17592186287823} {:db/id 17592186292841} {:db/id 17592186295168} {:db/id 17592186295169} {:db/id 17592186295170} {:db/id 17592186295171} {:db/id 17592186326925} {:db/id 17592186342070} {:db/id 17592186342071} {:db/id 17592186378566} {:db/id 17592186379355} {:db/id 17592186400338}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining Whether Three Vectors are Coplanar"} :step/id #uuid "58a570ee-c7cc-5be3-bfd4-c8e0901c10f3" :step/math-academy-id 464359 :step/next {:db/id 17592186106929}} {:db/id 17592186106929 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107085 :tutorial/content "Sometimes, we are not given the vectors that represent the sides of a parallelepiped. To compute the volume of a parallelepiped given the vertices, we can still use a similar process as before. The only difference is that we have to start by computing the displacement vectors between the points.

$$
V =  |\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})|
$$

But why is this formula true? To understand why, remember that the volume of a parallelepiped can be obtained by multiplying the area of the base by the height.

As we can see in the diagram below, 

- the area of the base is given by $A = | \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c} |,$ and

- the height is given by $h = |\text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}}\:\mathbf{a}|.$

![](images/cf/cfc492127bed6d6929518a708288691c5fe79e1842be6ecf92666bed6b03200b.png)

To compute the volume, we will multiply the area of the base by the height. First, though, let's write down the expression for the height:

$$
\begin{aligned}h & =|{\text{proj}}_{b\times c}\,a| \\  & =|\frac{a\cdot (b\times c)}{|b\times c|}| \\  & =\frac{|a\cdot (b\times c)|}{|b\times c|}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, multiplying the area of the base by the height, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =A\cdot h \\  & =|b\times c|\cdot \frac{|a\cdot (b\times c)|}{|b\times c|} \\  & =|a\cdot (b\times c)|.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6b371cde-1beb-5aa2-b564-0bae79e2faf1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3309 :tutorial/title "Proof That the Volume of a Parallelepiped is Given by the Absolute Value of the Triple Product"} :step/id #uuid "e1974a4e-dd77-5808-a604-05fb1fa36604" :step/math-academy-id 464366}] :activity/title "Volumes of Parallelepipeds" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186105964} {:db/id 17592186106925 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107078 :tutorial/content "Geometrically, the absolute value of the scalar triple product $\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})$ represents the volume enclosed by the parallelepiped whose sides are formed by the three vectors $\mathbf{a},$ $\mathbf{b},$ and $\mathbf{c}.$

$$
V =  |\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})|
$$

But why is this formula true? To understand why, remember that the volume of a parallelepiped can be obtained by multiplying the area of the base by the height.

As we can see in the diagram below, 

- the area of the base is given by $A = | \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c} |,$ and

- the height is given by $h = |\text{proj}_{\mathbf{b}\times\mathbf{c}}\:\mathbf{a}|.$

![](images/cf/cfc492127bed6d6929518a708288691c5fe79e1842be6ecf92666bed6b03200b.png)

To compute the volume, we will multiply the area of the base by the height. First, though, let's write down the expression for the height:

$$
\begin{aligned}h & =|{\text{proj}}_{b\times c}\,a| \\  & =|\frac{a\cdot (b\times c)}{|b\times c|}| \\  & =\frac{|a\cdot (b\times c)|}{|b\times c|}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, multiplying the area of the base by the height, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =A\cdot h \\  & =|b\times c|\cdot \frac{|a\cdot (b\times c)|}{|b\times c|} \\  & =|a\cdot (b\times c)|.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6b371cde-1beb-5aa2-b564-0bae79e2faf1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3309 :tutorial/title "Proof That the Volume of a Parallelepiped is Given by the Absolute Value of the Triple Product"} :step/id #uuid "e1974a4e-dd77-5808-a604-05fb1fa36604" :step/math-academy-id 464366} {:db/id 17592186107084 :tutorial/content "We have been using the fact that the volume of a parallelepiped spanned by the vectors $\mathbf{a},$ $\mathbf{b},$ and $\mathbf{c}$ is given by the absolute value of the triple product:

:knowledge-point/title "Finding the Greatest Common Factor when it is a Positive Constant"}] :question/problem "Find the greatest common factor of $2x$ and $10y$." :question/worked-solution "First, we decompose each expression into its separate factors. We express each constant as a product of its prime factors, and we treat each variable in the product as a separate factor.

$$
\begin{aligned}
2x &= 2 \cdot x \\
10y &= 2 \cdot 5 \cdot y
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we pair off the individual factors as much as possible.

$$
\begin{aligned}
2x &= 2_(―) \cdot x \\
10y &= 2_(―) \cdot 5 \cdot y
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take one factor from each pair. Here, there is only one pair, so we just need to take that factor. There are no other factors to multiply it with.

$$
\textrm{GCF}(2x,10y) = {\color{red}{2}}
$$

Thus, the greatest common factor of $2x$ and $10y$ is $2$."} {:db/id 17592186049540} {:db/id 17592186051009} {:db/id 17592186055262 :question/id #uuid "a55a0a89-297f-5d5a-a1f3-c71eaea34bbf" :question/math-academy-id "q-41033"} {:db/id 17592186055400 :question/id #uuid "01ad12c4-f22c-56f0-b0f2-d390331683bd" :question/math-academy-id "q-57113"} {:db/id 17592186054688 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054589 :question/id #uuid "f4d78520-1050-5ca1-a2da-1b813269dd9d" :question/math-academy-id "e-817"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "01ac1e8c-128c-5c13-b845-105092ae74d6" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055263 :question/id #uuid "f4a27e27-1ddc-58be-a98b-78ebb8d60073" :question/math-academy-id "q-41041"} {:db/id 17592186055265 :question/id #uuid "7422544d-da55-5401-a42f-82b630a0bed8" :question/math-academy-id "q-41044"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Greatest Common Factor when it Contains Variables"} {:db/id 17592186054589 :question/id #uuid "f4d78520-1050-5ca1-a2da-1b813269dd9d" :question/math-academy-id "e-817" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186054688 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "01ac1e8c-128c-5c13-b845-105092ae74d6" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Greatest Common Factor when it Contains Variables"}] :question/problem "Find the $\textrm{GCF}$ of $16a$ and $4a$." :question/worked-solution "First, we decompose each expression into its separate factors. We express each constant as a product of its prime factors, and we treat each variable in the product as a separate factor.

$$
\begin{aligned}
16a &= 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot a \\
4a &= 2 \cdot 2 \cdot a
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we pair off the individual factors as much as possible.

$$
\begin{aligned}
16a &= 2_(―) \cdot 2_(―) \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot a_(―) \\
4a &= 2_(―) \cdot 2_(―) \cdot a_(―)
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take one factor from each pair and multiply.

$$
\textrm{GCF}(16a, 4a) = \underline{2} \cdot \underline{2} \cdot \underline{a} = 4a
$$"} {:db/id 17592186055263 :question/id #uuid "f4a27e27-1ddc-58be-a98b-78ebb8d60073" :question/math-academy-id "q-41041"} {:db/id 17592186055265 :question/id #uuid "7422544d-da55-5401-a42f-82b630a0bed8" :question/math-academy-id "q-41044"} {:db/id 17592186054756 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054489 :question/id #uuid "7bc66df5-26b7-5eb0-b756-f8b086607209" :question/math-academy-id "e-1520"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ee5e58b3-f6d7-56e2-bccd-97095e94495e" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055264 :question/id #uuid "0aa2ff41-032b-53f0-9c0b-3afe911685cc" :question/math-academy-id "q-41043"} {:db/id 17592186055402 :question/id #uuid "a4fc75a2-c95b-5873-bc4c-c510fad07b06" :question/math-academy-id "q-57118"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Greatest Common Factor of Three Expressions"} {:db/id 17592186054489 :question/id #uuid "7bc66df5-26b7-5eb0-b756-f8b086607209" :question/math-academy-id "e-1520" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186054756 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ee5e58b3-f6d7-56e2-bccd-97095e94495e" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Greatest Common Factor of Three Expressions"}] :question/problem "Find the $\textrm{GCF}$ of $8a$, $4c$ and $12c$." :question/worked-solution "First, we decompose each expression into its separate factors. We express each constant as a product of its prime factors, and we treat each variable in the product as a separate factor.

$$
\begin{aligned}
8a &= 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 \cdot a \\
4c &= 2 \cdot 2 \cdot c \\
12c &= 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot c
\end{aligned}
$$

We now match up the individual factors as much as possible.

$$
\begin{aligned}
8a &= 2_(―) \cdot 2_(―) \cdot 2 \cdot a \\
4c &= 2_(―) \cdot 2_(―) \cdot c \\
12c &= 2_(―) \cdot 2_(―) \cdot 3 \cdot c
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take one factor from each pair and multiply.

$$
\textrm{GCF}(8a, 4c, 12c) = 2 \cdot 2 = 4
$$"} {:db/id 17592186055264 :question/id #uuid "0aa2ff41-032b-53f0-9c0b-3afe911685cc" :question/math-academy-id "q-41043"} {:db/id 17592186055402 :question/id #uuid "a4fc75a2-c95b-5873-bc4c-c510fad07b06" :question/math-academy-id "q-57118"} {:db/id 17592186054766 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054494 :question/id #uuid "aa1c4cbd-2086-5634-809f-43e4dd6becf9" :question/math-academy-id "e-1603"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "872ca3cb-830c-5af5-92f1-230611a8a693" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055198 :question/id #uuid "683dcc9c-40ec-5df0-bab1-816769e507a0" :question/math-academy-id "q-29713"} {:db/id 17592186055401 :question/id #uuid "8cc94d84-fd8c-5bca-8b34-d4ffd8bf2404" :question/math-academy-id "q-57116"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Greatest Common Factor when there are No Common Factors"} {:db/id 17592186054494 :question/id #uuid "aa1c4cbd-2086-5634-809f-43e4dd6becf9" :question/math-academy-id "e-1603" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186054766 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "872ca3cb-830c-5af5-92f1-230611a8a693" :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Greatest Common Factor when there are No Common Factors"}] :question/problem "What is the $\textrm{GCF}$ of $4a$ and $15b$?" :question/worked-solution "First, we decompose each expression into its separate factors. We express each constant as a product of its prime factors, and we treat each variable in the product as a separate factor.

$$
\begin{aligned}
4a &= 2 \cdot 2 \cdot a \\
15b &= 3 \cdot 5 \cdot b
\end{aligned}
$$

If we try to pair off the individual factors, we can't find any common factors. The only common factor is one. Thus,

$$
\textrm{GCF}(4a, 15b) = 1
$$"} {:db/id 17592186055198 :question/id #uuid "683dcc9c-40ec-5df0-bab1-816769e507a0" :question/math-academy-id "q-29713"} {:db/id 17592186055401 :question/id #uuid "8cc94d84-fd8c-5bca-8b34-d4ffd8bf2404" :question/math-academy-id "q-57116"} {:db/id 17592186048923} {:db/id 17592186050526} {:db/id 17592186051079} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186055656} :activity/id #uuid "0c86ff1c-1fc9-55e7-bf07-5e59726ce644" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049520 :topic/id #uuid "fc088d7c-dbfc-5873-80cb-82bec1e45e30" :topic/math-academy-id 85} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186055656 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055936 :tutorial/content "The **greatest common factor** (or $\textrm{GCF}$) of $12$ and $18x$ is the largest expression that will divide *both* $12$ and $18x$ with no remainder.

To find the GCF, we first decompose each expression into its separate factors. We express each constant as a product of its prime factors, and we treat each variable in the product as a separate factor.

$$
\begin{aligned}
12 &= 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \\
18x &= 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 \cdot x
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we pair off the individual factors as much as possible.

$$
\begin{aligned}
12 &= 2_(―) \cdot 2 \cdot 3_(―) \\
18x &= 2_(―) \cdot 3_(―) \cdot 3 \cdot x
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take one factor from each pair and multiply.

$$
\textrm{GCF}(12,18x) = {\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}3} = 6
$$

Thus, the greatest common factor of $12$ and $18x$ is $6$." :tutorial/id #uuid "b2b71877-6097-5d59-a2b8-7440bd0d5329" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1360 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186054927} {:db/id 17592186055656 :step/content {:db/id 17592186055936 :tutorial/content "The **greatest common factor** (or $\textrm{GCF}$) of $12$ and $18x$ is the largest expression that will divide *both* $12$ and $18x$ with no remainder.

To find the GCF, we first decompose each expression into its separate factors. We express each constant as a product of its prime factors, and we treat each variable in the product as a separate factor.

$$
\begin{aligned}
12 &= 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \\
18x &= 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 \cdot x
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we pair off the individual factors as much as possible.

$$
\begin{aligned}
12 &= 2_(―) \cdot 2 \cdot 3_(―) \\
18x &= 2_(―) \cdot 3_(―) \cdot 3 \cdot x
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take one factor from each pair and multiply.

$$
\textrm{GCF}(12,18x) = {\color{red}2} \cdot {\color{blue}3} = 6
$$

Thus, the greatest common factor of $12$ and $18x$ is $6$." :tutorial/id #uuid "b2b71877-6097-5d59-a2b8-7440bd0d5329" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1360 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c78d0b7d-678e-5655-a213-713eadefdc2c" :step/math-academy-id 2779 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055657}} {:db/id 17592186055936 :tutorial/content "The **greatest common factor** (or $\textrm{GCF}$) of $12$ and $18x$ is the largest expression that will divide *both* $12$ and $18x$ with no remainder.

Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform $L$ to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a system with variables ${X}_{1}(s)=L{{x}_{1}(t)}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L{{x}_{2}(t)}.$ In terms of the parameter $s,$ the solution of the new system is

$\,{X}_{2}(s)=$ {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "First, we find the Laplace transforms of both sides of each equation in our system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}L{{x}_{1}^{′}(t)}=L{-2{x}_{1}(t)} \\ L{{x}_{2}^{′}(t)}=L{-3{x}_{1}(t)+4{x}_{2}(t)}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}sL{{x}_{1}(t)}-{x}_{1}(0)=-2L{{x}_{1}(t)} \\ sL{{x}_{2}(t)}-{x}_{2}(0)=-3L{{x}_{1}(t)}+4L{{x}_{2}(t)}\end{aligned}
$$

which simplifies to:

$$
{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)-3=-2{X}_{1}(s) \\ s{X}_{2}(s)+4=-3{X}_{1}(s)+4{X}_{2}(s)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${X}_{1}(s)=L{{x}_{1}(t)}$ and ${X}_{2}(s)=L{{x}_{2}(t)}.$

Now, solving the first equation for ${X}_{1}(s),$ we get 

$$
s{X}_{1}(s)-3=-2{X}_{1}(s)\,⟹\,{X}_{1}(s)=\frac{3}{s+2}.
$$

Substituting this in the second equation and solving for ${X}_{2}(s)$ gives

$$
s{X}_{2}(s)+4=-3(\frac{3}{s+2})+4{X}_{2}(s)\,⟹\,{X}_{2}(s)=\frac{-4s-17}{(s-4)(s+2)}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186304963 :question/id #uuid "daf5c29f-5732-5955-b4c0-e9cfb924874e" :question/math-academy-id "q-331940"} {:db/id 17592186433218 :question/id #uuid Consider the initial value problem above. By applying the Laplace transform to both sides of each equation in our system, we get a transformed system with the solution 

$$
{X}_{1}(s)=L{{x}_{1}(t)}=\frac{1}{s}+\frac{4}{s-6},\,{X}_{2}(s)=L{{x}_{2}(t)}=\frac{5}{s}-\frac{4}{s-6}.
$$

Find the solution to the original initial value problem.

$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1+4{e}^{6t} \\ 5-4{e}^{6t}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]{e}^{6t}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049381} {:answer-field/id #uuid "faed85bb-89ce-5a06-b08b-d84b4c3cd7a9" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} **Step 1**. In the initial value problem above, we apply the Laplace transform $\mathcal{L}$ to both sides of each equation.

First, we find the Laplace transforms of both sides of each equation in our system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}L\{{x}_{1}^{′}(t)\}=L\{5{x}_{1}(t)\} \\ L\{{x}_{2}^{′}(t)\}=L\{-2{x}_{1}(t)+6{x}_{2}(t)\}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}sL\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-{x}_{1}(0)=5L\{{x}_{1}(t)\} \\ sL\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-{x}_{2}(0)=-2L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+6L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}\end{aligned}
$$

which can be simplified to the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)+3=5{X}_{1}(s) \\ s{X}_{2}(s)-2=-2{X}_{1}(s)+6{X}_{2}(s)\end{aligned}
$$

where $X_1(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_1(t) \right\}$ and $X_2(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_2(t) \right\}.$

**Step 2**. Now, solving the first equation for $X_1(s),$ we get

$$
s X_1(s) +  3 = 5 X_1(s)
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
X_1(s) = -\dfrac{3}{s-5}.
$$

Substituting this in the second equation and solving for $X_2(s),$ we have

$$
s X_2(s) -  2 = -2\left(-\dfrac{3}{s-5}\right) + 6 X_2(s) 
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
X_2(s) = \dfrac{2s-4}{(s-5)(s-6)}.
$$

**Step 3**. To find $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t)$ satisfying the original initial value problem, we apply the inverse Laplace transform to $X_1(s)$ and $X_2(s){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{1}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{-\frac{3}{s-5}\} \\  & =-3{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-5}\} \\  & =-3{e}^{5t} \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{2}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{2s-4}{(s-5)(s-6)}\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{8}{s-6}-\frac{6}{s-5}\} \\  & =8{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-6}\}-6{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-5}\} \\  & =8{e}^{6t}-6{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3{e}^{5t} \\ 8{e}^{6t}-6{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 8\end{aligned}]{e}^{6t}+[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -6\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a475ed27-9529-52d2-85cb-9e8827c5b45e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14201 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "648d1a99-8c25-5200-8b95-382792dca052" "aa736c0f-1eaa-5601-a02e-62159a1f73b2" :step/math-academy-id 590683} {:db/id 17592186167890 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168031 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we'll learn how to use Laplace transforms to solve homogeneous systems like the one below.
![](images/66/66eb9ce1b87b67ba550fc0b76493b775bf2b2e67be257b9fe9974db9d53cdffa.svg)

The process can be split into three steps.

- **Step 1.** Apply the Laplace transform $\mathcal{L}$ to both sides of each equation, to get a system with variables 

$$
X_1(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_1(t) \right\} \qquad \text{and} \qquad X_2(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_2(t) \right\}.
$$

- **Step 2.** Solve the obtained system for variables 

$$
X_1(s) \qquad \text{and} \qquad X_2(s).
$$

- **Step 3.** To find the initial variables

$$
x_1(t) \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_2(t)
$$

satisfying the original initial value problem, apply the inverse Laplace transform to 

$$
X_1(s) \qquad \text{and} \qquad X_2(s).
$$

![](images/66/66eb9ce1b87b67ba550fc0b76493b775bf2b2e67be257b9fe9974db9d53cdffa.svg)

The process can be split into three steps.

- **Step 1.** Apply the Laplace transform $\mathcal{L}$ to both sides of each equation, to get a system with variables 

$$
X_1(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_1(t) \right\} \qquad \text{and} \qquad X_2(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_2(t) \right\}.
$$

- **Step 2.** Solve the obtained system for variables 

$$
X_1(s) \qquad \text{and} \qquad X_2(s).
$$

- **Step 3.** To find the initial variables

$$
x_1(t) \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_2(t)
$$

satisfying the original initial value problem, apply the inverse Laplace transform to 

$$
X_1(s) \qquad \text{and} \qquad X_2(s).
$$

Let's see how this works in practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "98573e3a-ebcd-565e-8de7-a83e3deb9d09" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14610 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "f663bde1-a39c-5d4d-83fd-15b833a5cbea" :step/math-academy-id 590687 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167886}} {:db/id 17592186167886 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167982 :tutorial/content "![](images/44/44a90d0fa61d3643848f01479706cca752a00914b99185da5b8739c5e1cab182.svg)

**Step 1**. In the initial value problem above, we apply the Laplace transform $\mathcal{L}$ to both sides of each equation.

First, we find the Laplace transforms of both sides of each equation in our system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}L\{{x}_{1}^{′}(t)\}=L\{5{x}_{1}(t)\} \\ L\{{x}_{2}^{′}(t)\}=L\{-2{x}_{1}(t)+6{x}_{2}(t)\}\end{aligned}
$$

Using the derivative property of the Laplace transform, we obtain the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}sL\{{x}_{1}(t)\}-{x}_{1}(0)=5L\{{x}_{1}(t)\} \\ sL\{{x}_{2}(t)\}-{x}_{2}(0)=-2L\{{x}_{1}(t)\}+6L\{{x}_{2}(t)\}\end{aligned}
$$

which can be simplified to the following:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}s{X}_{1}(s)+3=5{X}_{1}(s) \\ s{X}_{2}(s)-2=-2{X}_{1}(s)+6{X}_{2}(s)\end{aligned}
$$

where $X_1(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_1(t) \right\}$ and $X_2(s) = \mathcal{L}\left\{  x_2(t) \right\}.$

**Step 2**. Now, solving the first equation for $X_1(s),$ we get

$$
s X_1(s) +  3 = 5 X_1(s)
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
X_1(s) = -\dfrac{3}{s-5}.
$$

Substituting this in the second equation and solving for $X_2(s),$ we have

$$
s X_2(s) -  2 = -2\left(-\dfrac{3}{s-5}\right) + 6 X_2(s) 
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
X_2(s) = \dfrac{2s-4}{(s-5)(s-6)}.
$$

**Step 3**. To find $x_1(t)$ and $x_2(t)$ satisfying the original initial value problem, we apply the inverse Laplace transform to $X_1(s)$ and $X_2(s){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{1}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{-\frac{3}{s-5}\} \\  & =-3{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-5}\} \\  & =-3{e}^{5t} \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={L}^{-1}\{{X}_{2}(s)\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{2s-4}{(s-5)(s-6)}\} \\  & ={L}^{-1}\{\frac{8}{s-6}-\frac{6}{s-5}\} \\  & =8{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-6}\}-6{L}^{-1}\{\frac{1}{s-5}\} \\  & =8{e}^{6t}-6{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the solution to the initial value problem:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) \\ {x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3{e}^{5t} \\ 8{e}^{6t}-6{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 8\end{aligned}]{e}^{6t}+[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -6\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a475ed27-9529-52d2-85cb-9e8827c5b45e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14201 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "648d1a99-8c25-5200-8b95-382792dca052" :step/math-academy-id 590676 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167887}} {:db/id 17592186167982 :tutorial/content "![](images/44/44a90d0fa61d3643848f01479706cca752a00914b99185da5b8739c5e1cab182.svg)

2xy^2,$ find the equation of the tangent line to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y) = (3,3).$" :question/worked-solution "The equation of the tangent line to the level curve $f(x,y) = k$ at the point $(x_0,y_0)$ can be expressed as

$$
\nabla f(x_0,y_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0, \: y-y_0 \rangle  = 0.
$$

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y) = (3,3)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\text{ }i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(6{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-2x{y}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(6{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-2x{y}^{2})\text{ }j \\  & =(12x-2{y}^{2})\text{ }i+(4y-4xy)\text{ }j \\ ∇\,f(3,3) & =(12(3)-2(3)^{2})i+(4(3)-4(3)(3))j \\  & =18\,i-24\,j \\  & =⟨18,-24⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the Cartesian equation of the tangent to the level curve that passes through the point $(x_0,y_0)=(3,3)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨x-{x}_{0},\,y-{y}_{0}⟩ & =0 \\ ∇f(3,3)\cdot ⟨x-3,\,y-3⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨18,-24⟩\cdot ⟨x-3,\,y-3⟩ & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We can leave our answer in this form. Or, if we want to leave our final answer in Cartesian form, we expand the dot product and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}18(x-3)-24(y-3) & =0 \\ 18x-24y+18 & =0 \\ 3x-4y+3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,1)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
\mathbf t(1,1) = f_y(1,1) \ \mathbf i - f_x(1,1) \ \mathbf j
$$

So, we calculate $\mathbf t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-3xy+4y)\text{ }i-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-3xy+4y)\text{ }j \\  & =(-3x+4)\text{ }i-(2x-3y)\text{ }j \\ t(1,1) & =(-3(1)+4)\text{ }i-(2(1)-3(1))\text{ }j \\  & =1\,i-(-1)\,j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $\mathbf i +\mathbf j,$ as shown in the diagram below.

:question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x{e}^{{y}^{2}+1} & =e-y \\ x{e}^{{y}^{2}+1}+y & =e\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=x{e}^{{y}^{2}+1}+y,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=e.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,0)$ can be computed as follows:

$$
t(1,0)={f}_{y}(1,0)i-{f}_{x}(1,0)j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{{y}^{2}+1}+y)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{{y}^{2}+1}+y)j \\  & =(2xy{e}^{{y}^{2}+1}+1)i-{e}^{{y}^{2}+1}\,j \\ t(1,0) & =(2(1)(0){e}^{0+1}+1)i-{e}^{0+1}\,j \\  & =i-e\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our tangent vector is $i-e\,j.$"} {:db/id 17592186323918 :question/id #uuid "12b276e2-b703-55f7-94b8-069326b3f510" :question/math-academy-id "q-37516"} {:db/id 17592186339107 :question/id tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $\mathbf{j}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}6xy+3{y}^{2} & =7+y-3{x}^{2} \\ 6xy+3{y}^{2}-y+3{x}^{2} & =7\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y) = 6xy+3y^2 - y + 3x^2 ,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=7.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
\mathbf t(x,y) = f_y(x,y) \ \mathbf i - f_x(x,y) \ \mathbf j
$$

So, we calculate $\mathbf t(x,y)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\text{ }i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(6xy+3{y}^{2}-y+3{x}^{2})\,i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(6xy+3{y}^{2}-y+3{x}^{2})\,j \\  & =(6x+6y-1)\,i-(6y+6x)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $\mathbf{j},$ we must have $\mathbf t \cdot \mathbf j = 0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot j & =0 \\ ((6x+6y-1)\,i-(6y+6x)\,j)\cdot j & =0 \\ -6y-6x & =0 \\ y & =-x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=-x$ into the equation of our curve gives

$$
\begin{aligned}6xy+3{y}^{2} & =7+y-3{x}^{2} \\ 6x(-x)+3(-x)^{2} & =7+(-x)-3{x}^{2} \\ -6{x}^{2}+3{x}^{2} & =7-x-3{x}^{2} \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, if $x=7,$ we get $y=-7$ and the corresponding point is $(7,-7).$"} {:db/id 17592186124970 :question/id #uuid "fa8c1acf-fd5d-5946-ab8b-13077cafbbf0" :question/math-academy-id "q-36332"} $2xy-3{x}^{2}=-y$ is the tangent vector to the curve perpendicular to the vector $j?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2xy-3{x}^{2}=-y \\ 2xy-3{x}^{2}+y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=2xy-3{x}^{2}+y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$ 

A tangent vector to the level curve can be computed as follows:

$$
t(x,y)={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j
$$

So, we calculate $t(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y) & ={f}_{y}(x,y)\,i-{f}_{x}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-3{x}^{2}+y)i-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-3{x}^{2}+y)j \\  & =(2x+1)\,i-2(y-3x)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Since our tangent vector needs to be perpendicular to $j$, we must have $t\cdot j=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}t(x,y)\cdot j & =0 \\ ((2x+1)\,i-2(y-3x)\,j)\cdot j & =0 \\ -2(y-3x) & =0 \\ y & =3x\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $y=3x$ into the equation of our curve gives:  

$$
\begin{aligned}2xy-3{x}^{2}+y & =0 \\ 2x(3x)-3{x}^{2}+3x & =0 \\ 6{x}^{2}-3{x}^{2}+3x & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}+3x & =0 \\ 3x(x+1) & =0 \\ x & =0\,\text{or}\,x=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally:

- If $x=0$, we get $y=0$ and the corresponding point is $(0,0).$

- If $x=-1$, we get $y=-3$ and the corresponding point is $(-1,-3).$"} {:db/id 17592186373757 :question/id #uuid "3d9c5851-2645-50db-8b4e-b731824fd7d9" :question/math-academy-id "q-130225"} {:db/id :topic/math-academy-id 1940} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125292 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125733 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the equation of the **tangent line** to the ellipse 

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{12} + \dfrac{y^2}{4} =1
$$

 at the point $P(3,1).$

To solve this problem, we could find the slope of the line using techniques from single-variable calculus. However, we can also solve the problem by computing the gradient of a two-variable function.

Let's start by defining 

$$
f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^2}{12} + \dfrac {y^2}{4}.
$$

Then, the given ellipse is the level curve  $f(x,y)=1.$

Now, we know that $\nabla \! f(3,1)$ is a vector that's normal to the level curve $f(x,y)= 1$ at $P(3,1).$ So, it's also normal to the tangent line to our ellipse at $P.$

![](images/3d/3dc75e8fd4083af1bf90f46b2e875d5d552bffdc5c1cfaeabebef70f79f00828.png)

Suppose that $(x,y)$ is any point on that tangent line. Then $\mathbf v=\langle x - 3, y-1 \rangle$ is a vector that's parallel to the tangent line. So $\mathbf v$ must be also orthogonal to $\nabla f(3,1),$ and since the dot product of two orthogonal vectors is zero, we have that

$$
\nabla f(3,1)\,\cdot \,\langle x - 3, y-1 \rangle = 0.
$$

Now, computing $\nabla\! f$ and evaluating it at the point $P(3,1),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{x}{6},\frac{y}{2}⟩ \\ ∇\,f(3,1) & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the equation of our tangent, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(3,1)\cdot ⟨x-3,y-1⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩\cdot ⟨x-3,y-1⟩ & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}(x-3)+\frac{1}{2}(y-1) & =0 \\ (x-3)+(y-1) & =0 \\ x+y-4 & =0\end{aligned}

Let $f(x,y)$ be a function that's continuously differentiable at the point $P(x_0,y_0).$   If  $\nabla f(x_0, y_0)$ is not the zero vector, then it is orthogonal to the tangent line to the level curve 

$$
f(x,y)= f(x_0,y_0)
$$

at the point $P.$ The equation of the tangent can then be written as

$$
\nabla\! f (x_0,y_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0,y-y_0\rangle  = 0.
$$

Writing this explicitly, we get

$$
f_x(x_0,y_0)(x-x_0) + f_y(x_0,y_0)(y-y_0)   = 0.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e9c2ee0b-08cf-5f42-bf09-f80dcd82051d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3866 :tutorial/title "Tangent Line to a Level Curve"} :step/id #uuid "2e3c389c-2b5c-55ca-92a8-e52fcbcf9f84" :step/math-academy-id 22698 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125293}}] :activity/title "Tangent Lines to Level Curves" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124732} {:db/id 17592186125292 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125733 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the equation of the **tangent line** to the ellipse 

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{12} + \dfrac{y^2}{4} =1
$$

 at the point $P(3,1).$

To solve this problem, we could find the slope of the line using techniques from single-variable calculus. However, we can also solve the problem by computing the gradient of a two-variable function.

Let's start by defining 

$$
f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^2}{12} + \dfrac {y^2}{4}.
$$

Then, the given ellipse is the level curve  $f(x,y)=1.$

Now, we know that $\nabla \! f(3,1)$ is a vector that's normal to the level curve $f(x,y)= 1$ at $P(3,1).$ So, it's also normal to the tangent line to our ellipse at $P.$

![](images/3d/3dc75e8fd4083af1bf90f46b2e875d5d552bffdc5c1cfaeabebef70f79f00828.png)

Suppose that $(x,y)$ is any point on that tangent line. Then $\mathbf v=\langle x - 3, y-1 \rangle$ is a vector that's parallel to the tangent line. So $\mathbf v$ must be also orthogonal to $\nabla f(3,1),$ and since the dot product of two orthogonal vectors is zero, we have that

$$
\nabla f(3,1)\,\cdot \,\langle x - 3, y-1 \rangle = 0.
$$

Now, computing $\nabla\! f$ and evaluating it at the point $P(3,1),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{x}{6},\frac{y}{2}⟩ \\ ∇\,f(3,1) & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the equation of our tangent, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(3,1)\cdot ⟨x-3,y-1⟩ & =0 \\ ⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩\cdot ⟨x-3,y-1⟩ & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}(x-3)+\frac{1}{2}(y-1) & =0 \\ (x-3)+(y-1) & =0 \\ x+y-4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7a9dede8-0672-56eb-9084-cf581e3fb05f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2496 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7cc9655e-83bb-5f85-8c20-add1d27fb5e0" :step/math-academy-id 11184 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125464}} {:db/id 17592186125733 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the equation of the **tangent line** to the ellipse

To do that, we put a plus sign between the two, collect like terms, and then simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(6x^{2} + x + 1) + (2x^{2} - 3x + 6) &=  \\
6x^{2} + x + 1 + 2x^{2} - 3x + 6 &=  \\
6x^{2} + 2x^{2}_(⏟)_(x^{2}terms) + x - 3x^(⏞)^(xterms) + 1 + 6_(⏟)_(constants) &=  \\
(6 + 2)x^{2} + (1 - 3)x + 7 &=  \\
&= 8x^{2} - 2x + 7
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "f6745611-70da-526a-9a6c-143b072c13c2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8873 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7baea5d5-f521-54dc-aa2f-ff6e04e9e58c" :step/math-academy-id 521385 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055788}} {:db/id 17592186055788 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054773 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054472 :question/id #uuid "c14b3658-bbe4-53f8-a0b6-377b2586f099" :question/math-academy-id "e-14305"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e4a8dbbc-4d43-53de-97fa-59eb5c78d8b7" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049538}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186054962} {:db/id 17592186055146} {:db/id 17592186055299}] :knowledge-point/title "Adding Polynomials"} :step/id #uuid "46ff7c1c-0ad5-5a99-a07f-4743ea906700" :step/math-academy-id 521386 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055789}} {:db/id 17592186055789 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054774 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054473 :question/id #uuid "c2e54fec-23da-515b-994b-8fa0601b5a9d" :question/math-academy-id "e-14307"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ad65c6c8-d57c-520e-9e2d-c1dc59979e19" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055106} {:db/id 17592186055111} {:db/id 17592186055441}] :knowledge-point/title "Adding Polynomials Expressed as Functions"} :step/id #uuid "d2d2808c-5375-5c39-8d76-ed44abc7a434" :step/math-academy-id 521390 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055790}} {:db/id 17592186055790 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056068 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to *subtract* the polynomial $2x^2 + x$ from the polynomial $6x^2 - 3x +1$. To do that, we start by putting a minus sign between the two:

$$
(6x^2 - 3x +1) - (2x^2 + x)
$$

Here, we need to remember to distribute the minus sign. Once we've done that, we can collect like terms and then simplify as usual:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(6x^{2} - 3x + 1) - (2x^{2} + x) &=  \\
6x^{2} - 3x + 1 - 2x^{2} - x &=  \\
6x^{2} - 2x^{2} - 3x - x + 1 &=  \\
(6 - 2)x^{2} + (-3 - 1)x + 1 &=  \\
&= 4x^{2} - 4x + 1
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "90da9a1a-3727-51e9-ad38-7db8b7ed3e20" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8875 :tutorial/title "The Difference of Two Polynomials"} :step/id #uuid "a0375f2a-c27c-50dc-b2aa-7d86343e6e08" :step/math-academy-id 521394 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055791}} {:db/id 17592186055791 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054775 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054474 :question/id #uuid "4d680b83-1789-5786-92a5-313073b253c4" :question/math-academy-id "e-14310"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "aa0b0b8a-3d45-5602-a842-a1b7f50ffcea" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049939}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055112} {:db/id 17592186055472} {:db/id 17592186055485}] :knowledge-point/title "Subtracting Polynomials"} :step/id #uuid "015841f6-ea30-5123-b4ff-814780c357f9" :step/math-academy-id 521395 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055792}} {:db/id 17592186055792 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054776 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054475 :question/id #uuid "4c4aa55e-a77c-58c5-a3f7-74a7cf57eb48" :question/math-academy-id "e-14315"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "abd67412-213b-5019-94ca-c4fb8bb39fc1" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186054963} {:db/id 17592186055107} {:db/id 17592186055147}] :knowledge-point/title "Subtracting Polynomials Expressed as Functions"} :step/id #uuid "7c7ca7d9-ecb0-5c71-a008-51cd9a46b417" :step/math-academy-id 521399}] :activity/title "Adding and Subtracting Polynomials" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186054925} {:db/id 17592186055787 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056067 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we have the two polynomials $6x^2 + x +1$ and $2x^2 - 3x + 6$, and we want to add them. To do that, we put a plus sign between the two, collect like terms, and then simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(6x^{2} + x + 1) + (2x^{2} - 3x + 6) &=  \\

:tutorial/content "Let's think about how to factor the following trinomial:

$$
x^2 + 7x + 12
$$

This trinomial is neither a perfect square nor a difference of squares. In such cases, the factoring process requires a little trial and error.

We can factor this trinomial in four steps:

- **Step 1:** Find the factor pairs of the constant term $(12)$:The factor pairs of $12$ are
$(1, 12), (2, 6), (3, 4)$.
- **Step 2:** Determine which of these factor pairs add up to the coefficient of the linear term $(7)$:
$\begin{bmatrix}1 + 12|= 13 & \cdot \\ 2 + 6|= 8 & \cdot \\ 3 + 4|= 7 & ✓\end{bmatrix}$
- **Step 3:** Using the factor pair identified in the previous step, write the linear term as $7x=3x+4x$:
$x^{2} + 7x + 12|=; x^{2} + 3x + 4x_(⏟)_(7x) + 12$
- **Step 4:** Factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately and then factor the expression completely:
$x^{2} + 3x + 4x + 12|=; (x^{2} + 3x) + (4x + 12)|=; x(x + 3) + 4(x + 3)|=; (x + 4)(x + 3)$

And we're done!

Before we continue, note the following:

- The process carried out in step 4 is sometimes called **factoring by grouping.** This is because we group two sets of terms and factor them individually before factoring the entire expression.
- We can check that our answer is correct by multiplying out the factors:
$(x + 4)(x + 3)|= x(x + 3) + 4(x + 3); = x^{2} + 3x + 4x + 12; = x^{2} + 7x + 12✓$" :tutorial/id #uuid "90a8aa34-4549-57c2-bdc2-24cc962cd306" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8891 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "add682be-a6dd-51b0-a261-ba8a3f84b958" :step/math-academy-id 178072 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055609}} {:db/id 17592186055609 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054658 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054476 :question/id #uuid "1e0116a2-6f90-5b57-97c1-6a64b45c9cef" :question/math-academy-id "e-14343"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3c9ba00d-9171-5732-8539-2e2943cce58e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048351} {:db/id 17592186051017}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055108} {:db/id 17592186055495} {:db/id 17592186055497} {:db/id 17592186233563} {:db/id 17592186233570} {:db/id 17592186233577}] :knowledge-point/title "Factoring Trinomials With Positive Coefficients"} :step/id #uuid "072ef290-5a3e-575d-a0fd-7d8084343f23" :step/math-academy-id 178073 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055610}} {:db/id 17592186055610 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056070 :tutorial/content "Let's now consider the following trinomial:

$$
x^2 - 2x - 8
$$

Notice that the constant term $(-8)$ is *negative*. So, when writing down our factor pairs, one number will always be positive, and the other will always be negative.

So, first, we write down all factor pairs of $-8{:}$

$$
(1,-8), (-1, 8), (2,-4), (-2, 4)
$$

Now, we find which factor pair adds up to the coefficient of the linear term $(-2)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{bmatrix}1 + (-8) &= -7 & \cdot \\ (-1) + 8|= 7 & \cdot \\ 2 + (-4)|=-2 & ✓ \\ (-2) + 4|= 2 & \cdot\end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$

Using the factor pair identified above, write the linear term as

$$
-2x = 2x-4x
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{2} - 2x - 8 &=  \\
&= x^{2} + 2x - 4x - 8
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately, and then factor the expression completely:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{2} + 2x - 4x - 8 &=  \\
(x^{2} + 2x) + (-4x - 8) &=  \\
x(x + 2) - 4(x + 2) &=  \\
&= (x - 4)(x + 2)
\end{aligned}
$$

Let's see another example." :tutorial/id #uuid "3b5a5752-232b-5714-b74a-1e50c4210b83" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8894 :tutorial/title "Trinomials With Negative Constants"} :step/id #uuid "232a2780-b6bf-56f2-b607-6b8d27ae3f25" :step/math-academy-id 178077 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055611}} {:db/id 17592186055611 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054659 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054478 :question/id #uuid "41c3e610-0259-59db-9494-3af6f47c7360" :question/math-academy-id "e-14350"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ac258511-5028-5fc8-9843-99309b36a38e" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055130} {:db/id 17592186055229} {:db/id 17592186055231}] :knowledge-point/title "Factoring Trinomials With Negative Constants"} :step/id #uuid "47e26748-840d-518f-8679-595bc9b0406d" :step/math-academy-id 178078 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055612}} {:db/id 17592186055612 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056076 :tutorial/content "Remember that to factor a quadratic expression, we must find a factor pair of the constant term that adds to the coefficient of the linear term.

With that in mind, let's factor the following trinomial:

$$
x^2 - 7x+12
$$

Notice that,

- the constant term $(12)$ is *positive*, while
- the coefficient of the linear term $(-7)$ is *negative*.

Since the constant is *positive* and the coefficient of the linear term is *negative*, we must first consider the *negative* factor pairs of the constant term $(12)$. These are as follows:

$$
(-1,-12),\qquad (-2,-6),\qquad (-3,-4)
$$

For each pair, their *product* is positive, and their *sum* is negative, which is what we want.

Now, we find which factor pair adds up to the coefficient of the linear term $(-7)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\begin{bmatrix}(-1) + (-12) &= -13 & \cdot \\ (-2) + (-6)|=-8 & \cdot \\ (-3) + (-4)|=-7 & ✓\end{bmatrix}
\end{aligned}
$$

Using the factor pair identified in the previous step, write the linear term as

$$
-7x = -3x - 4x
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{2} - 7x + 12 &=  \\
&= x^{2} - 3x - 4x + 12
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x^{2} - 3x - 4x + 12 &=  \\
(x^{2} - 3x) + (-4x + 12) &=  \\
&= x(x - 3) + 4(-x + 3)
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to get a *common* factor in both terms, we take an additional factor of $-1$ from the second term:

$$
x(x - 3) - 4(x - 3)
$$

Now that we have a common factor of $(x-3)$, we factor the expression fully in the usual way:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x(x - 3) - 4(x - 3) &=  \\
&= (x - 3)(x - 4)
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "25f481d5-38d8-5f35-95fc-dd74f97d0394" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9504 :tutorial/title "Trinomials With Negative Linear Coefficients and Positive Constants"} :step/id #uuid "47589875-8a7f-5cea-a2cf-0da701bb35ac" :step/math-academy-id 178082 :step/next {:db/id 17592186055613}} {:db/id 17592186055613 :step/content {:db/id 17592186054660 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054477 :question/id #uuid "f51ebe90-e58a-5712-84b8-4367ed18d58e" :question/math-academy-id "e-14346"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "65a95770-9419-5a8f-b264-58cca3e3c0db" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186055109} {:db/id 17592186055131} {:db/id 17592186055496}] :knowledge-point/title "Factoring Trinomials With Negative Linear Coefficients and Positive Constants"} :step/id #uuid "87945626-63e1-5990-b1f8-6d13138cf85c" :step/math-academy-id 178083}] :activity/title "Factoring Trinomials" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186054931} {:db/id 17592186055608 :step/content {:db/id 17592186056069 :tutorial/content "Let's think about how to factor the following trinomial:

![](images/53/5351dc4269f0b0d04a8c94aa939cc32b333471752f009e5775c829896e63afdd.png)

The theorem can be written as

$$
c^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2}
$$

where

17592186079457 :step/content {:db/id 17592186079621 :tutorial/content "A **polynomial term** is a term where the variable contains a non-negative integer power. (The non-negative integers consist of the numbers $0$, $1$, $2$, $3$, and so on.)

Some examples of polynomial terms include

$$
x^2, \qquad \dfrac 1 3 x^6,\qquad x, \qquad 1
$$

Let's go through each one:

- $x^{\color{blue}2}$ is a polynomial term because the power of the variable is ${\color{blue}2}$, a non-negative integer.
- $\dfrac{1}{3} x^{\color{blue}6}$ is a polynomial term because the power of the variable is ${\color{blue}6}$, which is also a non-negative integer. The coefficient of $\dfrac 1 3$ isn't important.
- $x$ is a polynomial term because it can be thought of as $x^{\color{blue}1}$. So the power of the variable is ${\color{blue}1}$, which is a non-negative integer.
- Finally, $1$ is a polynomial term because it can be expressed as $1\cdot x^{\color{blue}0}$. So the power of the variable is ${\color{blue}0}$, which is a non-negative integer.

On the other hand, the following expressions are *not* polynomial terms because their powers are not non-negative integers:

$$
4x^{-2}, \qquad x^{1/3}, \qquad {\sqrt{\color{black}x}}, \qquad {\dfrac{\color{black}1}{x^3}}
$$

To see why, let's go through each one:

- $4x^{\color{red}-2}$ is not a polynomial term because the power of the variable is ${\color{red}-2}$, which is negative.
- $x^{\color{red}1/3}$ is not a polynomial term because the power of the variable is ${\color{red}1/3}$, which is not an integer.
- $\sqrt x$ is not a polynomial term because it can be written as $x^{\color{red}1/2}$. So the power of the variable is ${\color{red}1/2}$, which is not an integer.
- Finally, $\dfrac 1 {x^3}$ is not a polynomial term because it can be written as $x^{-\color{red}3}$. So the power of the variable is ${\color{red}-3}$, which is negative." :tutorial/id #uuid "a11e9fb3-6fe1-547c-996f-fb83d15a47d0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1578 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0500aa37-469a-53bd-a5da-8fbb0fe569cc" :step/math-academy-id 4106 :step/next {:db/id 17592186079458}} {:db/id 17592186079458 :step/content {:db/id 17592186078529 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186078153 :question/id #uuid "0690af9e-ae28-50a0-b2fd-0a9c3baaec3e" :question/math-academy-id "e-1280"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c12f648d-f276-5123-b6aa-b222ad108825" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049089} {:db/id 17592186050495}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186079068} {:db/id 17592186079149}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Polynomial Terms"} :step/id #uuid "ad32752d-72d3-5211-adbf-f50f0a51075b" :step/math-academy-id 4107 :step/next {:db/id 17592186079459}} {:db/id 17592186079459 :step/content {:db/id 17592186079622 :tutorial/content "A **polynomial** is a sum of polynomial terms, such as

She observes that the number of bacteria in the dish *triples* every hour. If there were $100$ bacteria initially, can she determine how many bacteria will be present after $3$ hours?

Starting with $100$ bacteria, she knows that this number *triples* after one hour. Remember that tripling means to multiply by a factor of $3$.

To get the number of bacteria after one hour, we multiply the initial amount by $3$:

$$
\color{blue}{100\cdot 3}
$$

I. $\textrm{cm}^2$

II. $\textrm{cm}^3$

III. $\textrm{kg}$" :question/worked-solution "We can measure length in centimeters $(\textrm{cm}).$ When measuring lengths in centimeters, volumes are measured in $\textrm{cm} \times \textrm{cm} \times \textrm{cm},$ which is usually written as $\textrm{cm}^3.$

17592186189383 :tutorial/content "**Area** measures how much space there is on a flat surface. In this lesson, we'll learn about the various measurement units of area and how they relate to units of length. 

Consider a square with sides of length $1\,\textrm{m},$ shown below. 

![](images/3f/3feaac95102a8a3014b7ab114adb97d5a0267a5c654c584bff03152801c807c2.png)

To find the area of a square, we multiply its side lengths. Therefore, the area of this square is equal to

$$
1\,\textrm{m}\times 1\,\textrm{m} = 1\,\textrm{m}^2.
$$

The unit of area $(\textrm m^2)$ we used is called a **square meter.** In this case, we say that the area of our square is **one square meter.**

In previous lessons, we learned that length can also be measured in kilometers $(\textrm{km}),$ centimeters $(\textrm{cm}),$ and millimeters $(\textrm{mm}).$ Each of these length units has a corresponding area unit:

- A square with sides of length $1\,\textrm{km}$ has an area of $1\,\textrm{km}^2,$ or **one square kilometer**.

- A square with sides of length $1\,\textrm{cm}$ has an area of $1\,\textrm{cm}^2,$ or **one square centimeter**.

- A square with sides of length $1\,\textrm{mm}$ has an area of $1\,\textrm{mm}^2,$ or **one square millimeter**.

The same idea applies when measuring area in customary units. For example:

- A square with sides of length $1\,\textrm{in}$ has an area of $1\,\textrm{in}^2,$ or **one square inch**.

- A square with sides of length $1\,\textrm{ft}$ has an area of $1\,\textrm{ft}^2,$ or **one square foot**." :tutorial/id #uuid "782bd823-d56b-501d-97cd-2346156da037" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6332 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "81a881d6-35a5-534b-ad14-ce4e42142162" :step/math-academy-id 38318 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189130}} {:db/id 17592186189125 :step/content {:db/id 17592186188302 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186188009 :question/id #uuid "5f153b4a-2706-5ff6-b0b3-65cfc29e1391" :question/math-academy-id "e-10163"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "09b56d66-4e96-56de-b3fa-747cb2e3487d" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050170}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186188533} {:db/id 17592186188922} {:db/id 17592186440900} {:db/id 17592186440901} {:db/id 17592186440903} {:db/id 17592186440904}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing an Area With the Correct Units"} :step/id #uuid "6f7ec5ae-5a69-500f-9fb4-8f461d1c2564" :step/math-academy-id 38328 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189242}} {:db/id 17592186189130 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189385 :tutorial/content "**Volume** measures how much three-dimensional space there is inside something. 

Consider a cube with sides of length $1\,\textrm{m},$ shown below. 

![](images/f0/f0006ee19c09fcf56ad032675f5f71ca8e49fc4c554a169e17bff0a09f2bbb6a.png)

To find the volume of a cube, we multiply its side lengths. Therefore, the volume of this cube is equal to

$$
1\,\textrm{m}\times 1\,\textrm{m}\times 1\,\textrm{m} = 1\,\textrm{m}^3.
$$

The unit of volume $(\textrm m^3)$ we used is called a **cubic meter.** In this case, we say that the volume of our cube is **one cubic meter.**

As with area, each unit of length has a corresponding volume unit. For example:

- A cube with sides of length $1\,\textrm{cm}$ has a volume of $1\,\textrm{cm}^3,$ or **one cubic centimeter**.

- A cube with sides of length $1\,\textrm{in}$ has a volume of $1\,\textrm{in}^3,$ or **one cubic inch**." :tutorial/id #uuid "ad0f170d-4023-5465-9263-b8826bdaa467" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6337 :tutorial/title "Units of Volume"} :step/id #uuid "9c654269-ba54-5587-a9b6-ba5cb053ac2d" :step/math-academy-id 38355 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189122}} {:db/id 17592186189141 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189389 :tutorial/content "A square is a special type of rectangle whose length and width are equal. For example, consider the square below.

![](images/a9/a92233299ba67fec2a7712c88afcabeff3973dda07afdd7f91c085c4564e2aa1.png)

We say that the **side length** of this square equals $3\,\textrm{m}.$

Since a square is a special type of rectangle, we find its area by multiplying its length and width. However, since its length and width are equal, we can find its area by *squaring* its side length:

Therefore, the area of the square is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =(3\,\text{m})^{2}\text{ } \\  & =3\,\text{m}\times 3\,\text{m} \\  & =(3\times 3)\times (\text{m}\times \text{m}) \\  & =9\,{\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4d7c3905-be55-58f4-8070-adad0bd8fef4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15346 :tutorial/title "Calculating Area"} :step/id #uuid "d695cf8d-6531-5468-8016-c6cf9749344f" :step/math-academy-id 633751 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189125}} {:db/id 17592186189242 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189433 :tutorial/content "A **cube** is a special type of rectangular solid whose length, width, and height are equal. 

![](images/e6/e696b4b9875052f18f394df4f0c6fb867b599a8484ac04acfca021ade9618a49.png)

We say that the **side length** of this cube equals $2\,\textrm{cm}.$

Since a cube is a special type of rectangular solid, we find its volume by multiplying its length, width, and height. However, since its length, width, and height are all equal, we can find its volume by *cubing* its side length:

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =(2\,\text{cm})^{3} \\  & =(2\,\text{cm})\times (2\,\text{cm})\times (2\,\text{cm}) \\  & =(2\times 2\times 2)\times (\text{cm}\times \text{cm}\times \text{cm}) \\  & =8\,{\text{cm}}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "15a41542-a66e-5d1f-889a-ca578f48bae4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7945 :tutorial/title "Calculating Volume"} :step/id #uuid "e659ead9-3e52-5de3-86a3-60522e000640" :step/math-academy-id 45706 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189123}}] :activity/title "Units of Area and Volume" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186188466} {:db/id 17592186189124 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189383 :tutorial/content "**Area** measures how much space there is on a flat surface. $$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4d7c3905-be55-58f4-8070-adad0bd8fef4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15346 :tutorial/title "Calculating Area"} :step/id #uuid "d695cf8d-6531-5468-8016-c6cf9749344f" :step/math-academy-id 633751 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189125}} {:db/id 17592186189123 :step/content {:db/id 17592186188301 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186188008 :question/id #uuid "94639d5a-c922-52f3-8e50-82d0e9a3dbad" :question/math-academy-id "e-10150"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "469f0c76-3641-5a56-82bb-9ac807ff2017" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050338}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186188523} {:db/id 17592186188571} {:db/id 17592186233496}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing a Volume With the Correct Units"} :step/id #uuid "3fc81ced-9831-5655-a85b-a4d4b3264016" :step/math-academy-id 38277} {:db/id 17592186189383 :tutorial/content "**Area** measures how much space there is on a flat surface. In this lesson, we'll learn about the various measurement units of area and how they relate to units of length. 

Consider a square with sides of length $1\,\textrm{m},$ shown below. 

![](images/3f/3feaac95102a8a3014b7ab114adb97d5a0267a5c654c584bff03152801c807c2.png)

To find the area of a square, we multiply its side lengths. Therefore, the area of this square is equal to

$$
1\,\textrm{m}\times 1\,\textrm{m} = 1\,\textrm{m}^2.
$$

The unit of area $(\textrm m^2)$ we used is called a **square meter.** In this case, we say that the area of our square is **one square meter.**

In previous lessons, we learned that length can also be measured in kilometers $(\textrm{km}),$ centimeters $(\textrm{cm}),$ and millimeters $(\textrm{mm}).$ Each of these length units has a corresponding area unit:

- A square with sides of length $1\,\textrm{km}$ has an area of $1\,\textrm{km}^2,$ or **one square kilometer**.

- A square with sides of length $1\,\textrm{cm}$ has an area of $1\,\textrm{cm}^2,$ or **one square centimeter**.

- A square with sides of length $1\,\textrm{mm}$ has an area of $1\,\textrm{mm}^2,$ or **one square millimeter**.

The same idea applies when measuring area in customary units. For example:

- A square with sides of length $1\,\textrm{in}$ has an area of $1\,\textrm{in}^2,$ or **one square inch**.

- A square with sides of length $1\,\textrm{ft}$ has an area of $1\,\textrm{ft}^2,$ or **one square foot**." :tutorial/id #uuid "782bd823-d56b-501d-97cd-2346156da037" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6332 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186189130 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189385 :tutorial/content "**Volume** measures how much three-dimensional space there is inside something. 

Consider a cube with sides of length $1\,\textrm{m},$ shown below. 

![](images/f0/f0006ee19c09fcf56ad032675f5f71ca8e49fc4c554a169e17bff0a09f2bbb6a.png)

To find the volume of a cube, we multiply its side lengths. Therefore, the volume of this cube is equal to

$$
1\,\textrm{m}\times 1\,\textrm{m}\times 1\,\textrm{m} = 1\,\textrm{m}^3.
$$

The unit of volume $(\textrm m^3)$ we used is called a **cubic meter.** In this case, we say that the volume of our cube is **one cubic meter.**

As with area, each unit of length has a corresponding volume unit. For example:

- A cube with sides of length $1\,\textrm{cm}$ has a volume of $1\,\textrm{cm}^3,$ or **one cubic centimeter**.

- A cube with sides of length $1\,\textrm{in}$ has a volume of $1\,\textrm{in}^3,$ or **one cubic inch**." :tutorial/id #uuid "ad0f170d-4023-5465-9263-b8826bdaa467" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6337 :tutorial/title "Units of Volume"} :step/id #uuid "9c654269-ba54-5587-a9b6-ba5cb053ac2d" :step/math-academy-id 38355 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189122}} {:db/id 17592186189125 :step/content {:db/id 17592186188302 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186188009 :question/id #uuid "5f153b4a-2706-5ff6-b0b3-65cfc29e1391" :question/math-academy-id "e-10163"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "09b56d66-4e96-56de-b3fa-747cb2e3487d" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050170}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186188533} {:db/id 17592186188922} {:db/id 17592186440900} {:db/id 17592186440901} {:db/id 17592186440903} {:db/id 17592186440904}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing an Area With the Correct Units"} :step/id #uuid "6f7ec5ae-5a69-500f-9fb4-8f461d1c2564" :step/math-academy-id 38328 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189242}} {:db/id 17592186189242 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189433 :tutorial/content "A **cube** is a special type of rectangular solid whose length, width, and height are equal.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & -1\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -4 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & -4 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{3}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{3} & \frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$

So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Computing $A-(-2)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{\lambda }_{2}I & =[\begin{aligned}-10 & 16 & 8 \\ -6 & 20 & 6 \\ -12 & 4 & 10\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & 16 & 8 \\ -6 & 22 & 6 \\ -12 & 4 & 12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ that we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & 16 & 8 & 0 \\ -6 & 22 & 6 & 0 \\ -12 & 4 & 12 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=-\frac{1}{8}{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-2{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ -6 & 22 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & -40 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+6{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 10 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd ones). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}={x}_{3}.$
Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ 0 \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 4 \\ 2 & -2 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 12\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$

![](images/2c/2c41221da0e4c0895928e65602e588f380452172e29d79f6e9f68ebb49e57807.svg)

In general, we have the following theorem:

*An $n\times n$ matrix $A$ is diagonalizable if and only if there exists a basis of $\mathbb{R}^n$ that consists of eigenvectors of $A$.*

Since eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues are linearly independent, we can also  conclude the following fact:

*If an $n\times n$ matrix $A$ has $n$ *distinct* eigenvalues (that is, $n$ simple roots of the corresponding characteristic equation), then there exists a basis of eigenvectors. Thus, the matrix is diagonalizable.*

![](images/ec/ecc57b51a49c8d1d6fbadd69908dbf6f48803cd6ca1f72ad189a1e5410c5d71c.svg)
are the respective eigenvectors. To find an invertible matrix $P$ and  a diagonal matrix $D$ such that $PDP^{-1} = A,$  we do the following: .

![](images/4f/4f878ce6a4b6f770cd520e22a8e4a3c6f8b3012b7de446bd3f533e61bda85a13.svg)

Now, to construct the matrix $P,$ we simply write the respective eigenvectors as columns: 

- the $1$st column is the eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda_1={\color{blue}-2},$

- the $2$nd column is the eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda_2={\color{red}1},$ and

- the $3$rd column is the eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda_3=-3.$

Therefore, we get

![](images/95/95c896911a6d54ea6385821846a3f0e4fc1a8f05f29e83b951ba270a3898938e.svg)

**Note:** If the matrix $A$ does not have $n$ distinct eigenvalues, it is not always possible to diagonalize it. $\displaystyle\int_2^0\mathbf f(t) \,\textrm{d}t= \left\langle -3, \: 2, \: 1 \right\rangle.$" :question/worked-solution "Let's reverse the limits of integration on the known result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t & =-{\int }_{2}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-⟨-3,\,2,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨3,\,-2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the vector addition rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)+⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{2}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{2}⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨3,\,-2,\,-1⟩+⟨t,\,-t,\,t⟩{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =⟨3,\,-2,\,-1⟩+⟨2,\,-2,\,2⟩\text{ } \\  & =⟨5,\,-4,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048563} {:db/id 17592186120556 :question/id #uuid "63279440-ddaa-5ce9-9454-481ab5b36e09" :question/math-academy-id "q-98093"} {:db/id 17592186120557 :question/id #uuid Adjacent Intervals Rule"}] :question/problem "Calculate 
$\displaystyle\int_{-1}^0\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t$
given that
$\displaystyle\int_0^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t= \left\langle \dfrac{3}{2}, \: 1, \: 3 \right\rangle$
and
$\displaystyle\int_{-1}^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t=\left\langle 0, \: 2, \: 6 \right\rangle.$" :question/worked-solution "Using the adjacent intervals, we get

$$
\int_{-1}^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t=\int_{-1}^0\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t+\int_0^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t .
$$

We can rearrange the above as follows:

$$
\int_{-1}^0\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t = 
\int_{-1}^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t - \int_0^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm{d}t
$$

Finally, using the given information, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨0,\,2,\,6⟩-⟨\frac{3}{2},\,1,\,3⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{3}{2},\,1,\,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186120180 :question/id #uuid "ae97662d-9168-5c3a-9fc4-a2e6f16a2143" :question/math-academy-id "q-32516"} {:db/id 17592186120555 :question/id #uuid "29982efe-8588-56f9-8a2e-657a512dab79" :question/math-academy-id "q-96943" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186119981 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d5287f63-6d1a-5710-8a71-df5d1ba09a00" :knowledge-point/title "Applying the Adjacent Intervals Rule"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "46bf7675-80a2-559b-8162-709a1a0d7f2f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "⟨10,\,6,\,1⟩" :db/id 17592186358358} {:answer/id #uuid "52b55dd5-256e-5209-86de-a9c9700d2990" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "⟨7,\,2,\,11⟩" :db/id 17592186358461} {:answer/id #uuid "90b044f6-737d-5f41-adc8-0bdca392f181" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "⟨-10,\,9,\,-11⟩" :db/id 17592186359017} {:answer/id #uuid "e6dcc4aa-84e5-52fb-b4ea-896d476393a3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "⟨9,\,1,\,-1⟩" :db/id 17592186359794} {:answer/id #uuid "ec412725-0d94-59a0-8fbf-bf17919c936a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "⟨-1,\,-3,\,11⟩" :db/id 17592186359855}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "90b044f6-737d-5f41-adc8-0bdca392f181" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "⟨-10,\,9,\,-11⟩" :db/id 17592186359017} :answer-field/id #uuid "e3e28b5a-b897-5ddd-a2bd-d85b9a72bf4f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186360402}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Calculate

given that 
$\displaystyle\int_0^1\mathbf f(t)\,\textrm d t = \mathbf i-3\,\mathbf j-4\,\mathbf k$ 
and 
$\mathbf c=\mathbf j-\mathbf k .$" :question/worked-solution "The cross-product rule states that

$$
{\int_0^1 } \mathbf c \times \mathbf f(t) \, \textrm d t =  \mathbf c \times {\int_0^1 } \mathbf f(t) \, \textrm d t  .
$$

 

Applying the cross-product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}c\times f(t)\,\text{d}t & =c\times {\int }_{0}^{1}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(j-k)\times (i-3\,j-4\,k) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -3 & -4\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -3 & -4\end{aligned}|i-|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}|j+|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}|k \\  & =(-4-3)i-(0+1)j+(0-1)k \\  & =-7\,i-\,j-\,k.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{a}^{p}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{p}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ef0617f3-7ee0-5300-8795-10adbdc19d3b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5178 :tutorial/title "The Adjacent Intervals Rule"} :step/id #uuid "84aafb0e-a1fc-506a-aa26-8b23e04c1756" :step/math-academy-id 32531 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120978}} {:db/id 17592186120792 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121081 :tutorial/content "Suppose that $\mathbf f(t)$ is a vector-valued function that is continuous on a closed interval $[a,b]$ and $\mathbf c$ is a constant vector. 
Then, the *products rules* are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{a}^{b}[c\cdot f(t)]\text{d}t=c\cdot ({\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t)\, & \text{dot product rule} \\ {\int }_{a}^{b}[c\times f(t)]\text{d}t=c\times {\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t\, & \text{cross product rule}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "2531e67a-b5ed-5052-a97f-34abca386c58" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5179 :tutorial/title "The Product Rules"} :step/id #uuid "60fca522-e8ee-530d-9936-cc7ec084b35f" :step/math-academy-id 32532 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120979}} {:db/id 17592186120976 :step/content {:db/id 17592186120995 :tutorial/content "Since the integration of vector functions is done component-by-component, the properties of integrals of vector functions are immediately inherited from those of the integrals of real-valued functions. 

Suppose that $\mathbf f(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t)$ are vector-valued functions that are continuous on a closed interval $[a,b],$ and $\alpha$ is a scalar. 
Then, the *vector addition and scalar multiplication rules* are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{a}^{b}(f(t)+g(t))\text{d}t={\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t\,+\,{\int }_{a}^{b}g(t)\,\text{d}t\, & \text{vector addition rule} \\ {\int }_{a}^{b}\alpha \,f(t)\,\text{d}t=\alpha \,{\int }_{a}^{b}f(t)\,\text{d}t\, & \text{scalar constant multiple rule}\end{aligned}
$$

  

For example, if $\mathbf f(t) = \left\langle t, \: \cos t\right\rangle$ and $\mathbf g(t) = \left\langle -t^2, \: \sin t \right\rangle,$ then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int [f(t)+2g(t)]\text{d}t & =\int f(t)\,\text{d}t+2\int g(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t+2\int ⟨-{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int t\,\text{d}t,\,\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩+⟨2\int -{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t,\,2\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+{C}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{C}_{2}⟩+⟨-\frac{2{t}^{3}}{3}+{C}_{3},\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{C}_{4}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3{t}^{2}-4{t}^{3}}{6},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

  

where $C_1, \, C_2, \, C_3, \, C_4$ are arbitrary real constants and ${\mathbf C} = \langle C_1+C_3, C_2+C_4 \rangle$ is a constant vector." :tutorial/id #uuid "b3d07bd2-8d66-5645-a140-c638f5e9f002" These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.
Students then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.
Applications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.

Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.
Students next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Concepts such as circulation, flux, and path independence lead to the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Green’s theorem, the divergence theorem, and Stokes’ theorem. These results form the mathematical framework underlying conservation laws and the differential and integral formulations of electromagnetic theory.
Applications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Students analyze motion using vector-valued functions, apply Newton’s second law to systems in the plane, and study work–energy relationships. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.
The course then returns to differential equations, extending earlier techniques to systems of linear differential equations. Students analyze dynamical systems using eigenvalues, phase portraits, and matrix methods, which appear in models of interacting systems such as coupled oscillators or predator–prey dynamics.
Laplace transforms are introduced as a powerful tool for solving linear differential equations with discontinuous inputs or initial conditions. Boundary value problems and Fourier series are then developed, providing mathematical techniques used to solve differential equations describing heat flow, vibrating strings, wave propagation, and other physical phenomena.
The course concludes with numerical methods for differential equations and advanced probability topics.
